A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
Any form of physical contact with others

My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: The social avoidance items are difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. These triggers imply avoidance of people linked to a discrete later-life event, but the trauma is chronic/developmental and caregiver-based; there is no corresponding trigger or appraisal content tying prior social contacts or specific intimacy-linked reminders to the abuse history.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: Intrusion Monitoring suggests fear of an intruder entering the home, which fits home-invasion or stalking trauma better than childhood caregiver physical abuse. With no accompanying memory or trigger content about nighttime entry, footsteps, doors, or home intrusion, this threat item is hard to explain from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: No Good Ahead and Outsider are broad, depressive or social-identity appraisals, whereas the other active content is dominated by vigilance, bodily threat detection, and sensory triggering. This combination is not impossible, but here the intimacy/social avoidance items appear to depend on relational shame or alienation that is otherwise underdeveloped and weakly connected to the trigger/threat pattern, reducing coherence.

issues.item: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore
issues.explanation: Given the formulation, Triggers and Negative Appraisals should be tightly linked, but the chosen triggers are mainly tactile/somatic/intrusive-memory cues while two maladaptive strategies focus on avoiding social contacts and intimacy. Those strategies are not well supported by the trigger set and feel targeted at a different symptom cluster than the one represented elsewhere.

# Clinical Vignette: Robert K.

Robert was sixty-six when he first walked into the office, moving with the careful precision of a man who had spent decades learning not to take up space. At fifty-eight, when his elderly mother had fallen and broken her hip, he had brought her to live with him and his wife, Margaret. Within weeks of her arrival, the old terrors had surfaced with a clarity that shocked him—not the vague anxiety of middle age, but the specific, embodied panic of a child pinned against cold tile.

His mother's hands had been cold, always cold. She would reach out to steady herself on his shoulder, and the shock of that chill against his skin would send him into a state of raw alarm that his conscious mind could not quite justify. When her fingers touched the back of his neck one morning as he poured her coffee, his heart had begun to race so violently he thought he might collapse. The sensation—that particular temperature, that invasive touch—pulled him backward across fifty years to a bathroom in a house he had tried to forget. And in that pulling backward, something crystallized: if these innocent gestures could trigger such terror, then people themselves—even Margaret, even his mother—must be sources of threat he could not predict or control. The logic felt airtight, inevitable. His father's hands, gripping him under cold running water as punishment for some small infraction, holding him there while his lungs burned and his small body convulsed with shock. The cold had been the instrument and the message: you are not safe, you are not in control, your body is not your own. Now, each time his mother's cold fingers found his shoulder or his own heart began to race unbidden, the old message returned with it: danger was real, it was close, and he could never fully protect himself from it. These triggers—the cold touch, the racing pulse, the unbidden flash of his father's face—each one sent a signal through his body that felt identical to the original threat. His nervous system could not distinguish between the memory and the present moment; when his mother's hand landed on his shoulder, his body registered it not as an innocent gesture but as an emergency, the same way it had registered the cold water fifty years ago. These moments of panic did not feel like echoes of the past—they felt like proof that the world remained as unsafe as it had always been.

The racing of his own heart became its own trigger. Each time it quickened—whether from the coffee he drank too fast or the anxiety that had begun to colonize his mornings—Robert felt the ground shift beneath him. The physical sensation itself was a warning, proof that danger was imminent. Every flutter of his pulse told him that he was right to be afraid, that his hypervigilance was not paranoia but clarity, the only honest way to read a world that had shown him its teeth long ago. And when his mother had reached for him again, or when Margaret had touched his arm in concern, his body had reacted before thought could intervene. He would flinch, sometimes cry out, his nervous system convinced that harm was coming. The intrusive memories came without warning too—a flash of his father's face, the cold, the helplessness—arriving suddenly while Robert was at his desk at work, leaving him shaking and unable to focus on code that had once been his refuge.

What had begun as isolated moments of discomfort had calcified into a set of certainties that now governed his days. Robert had come to believe that he had to be constantly vigilant, that the world contained threats he could not predict or control, that people—even those who loved him—could not be trusted with his vulnerability. The more he thought about these dangers, the more he noticed them everywhere. He began to scan rooms for potential weapons, for objects that could be used to harm him. He saw the kitchen knife differently now. He saw the belt Margaret hung by the door. These were not threats in any rational sense, but his mind had learned to read danger in the ordinary architecture of domestic life. And these vigilant observations only deepened his conviction that he was right to be afraid, that his constant carefulness was justified, necessary, the only thing keeping him safe.

To manage the panic, Robert had withdrawn. He stopped looking at his own body in the shower, unable to bear the sight of his skin without feeling exposed and vulnerable. He began declining invitations from the colleagues he had socialized with for years—the monthly dinners, the weekend hiking trips—telling himself that being around people meant being at risk, meant having to endure the possibility of unexpected touch. Most painfully, he had pulled away from Margaret's affection. But the very strategies that seemed to protect him had locked the threat in place. Each time he avoided a social gathering, each time he flinched away from Margaret's touch without staying long enough to discover that nothing terrible would happen, his nervous system received a message: the danger was real, the threat was ongoing, and his vigilance was the only thing keeping him alive. She had tried to understand, had asked what was wrong, but he could not explain that her hand on his back felt like a threat, that her attempt to comfort him felt like an invasion. The avoidance had seemed protective at first, a way to maintain control. But as weeks turned into months, the isolation had only intensified his belief that he was fundamentally damaged, permanently set apart from others, an outsider in his own marriage and his own life.

The cycle had tightened relentlessly. His avoidance of touch meant he remained hypervigilant to the possibility of it, scanning for the moment when someone might breach his boundary. His withdrawal from his body meant he was more attuned to its signals—every flutter of his heart felt dangerous, every unexpected sensation a harbinger. And each time he managed to avoid contact, each time he successfully isolated himself, the conviction that people could not be trusted, that he needed constant vigilance, grew stronger. Margaret had finally insisted he see someone, her own distress evident. Robert had agreed, though he remained uncertain whether anyone could help him understand why, after so many decades, the cold still had such power, and why the people closest to him now felt like the greatest threat of all.
